cim_eredeti: The Complete Guide to Embedding Models for Machine Learning
szoveg_eredeti:
In this article, you will learn how embedding models differ, what they cost to run at scale, and how to benchmark open-weight models on your own text data.

Text is an unstructured, rather messy form of data. Most importantly, machine learning algorithms do not understand raw text. Even the most modern and sophisticated language models today don’t handle text directly; they use numeric representations, one of which stands out: embedding vectors.

How do modern AI systems turn human language into such dense numerical vectors? The key bridge for this translation task is embedding models. Embedding models are trained to learn mappings from the semantic meaning behind text to high-dimensional coordinates, which makes efficient semantic search, text classification and clustering, and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) possible.

With so many embedding models available in today’s machine learning landscape, choosing the right solution can be overwhelming. This article focuses on what matters from a practitioner’s perspective. It is intended to guide you through choosing the right embedding model, understanding how aspects like dimensions and quantization can impact your application or pipeline, and benchmarking open-weight models on a given dataset.

In sum, not all models use the same approach to build embeddings. Before choosing one, make sure you understand their different characteristics to pick the right one for your job.

At this point, you may agree that selecting an embedding model is a key engineering decision. Bear in mind that the model dimensionality directly impacts memory footprint: take the scenario of turning a million text documents into 1536-dimensional embedding vectors, for instance. If each numerical value is stored as a 32-bit float, this would require approximately 6GB of RAM (1,000,000 × 1536 × 4 bytes) to hold them, plus the search index overhead!

This is why modern practitioners increasingly resort to a technique that helps keep solutions affordable and hardware-friendly: quantization. This technique compresses embeddings by carefully reducing their numerical precision.

Popular quantization techniques include scalar quantization, which reduces the memory footprint by 4x by turning 32-bit floats into 8-bit integers. Meanwhile, binary quantization is more drastic: it converts each float into a single bit, cutting memory by 32x, and it works best with models trained with binary embeddings in mind. It is not as accurate as scalar quantization, but it is a lot faster and still good enough for some applications.

Wondering how to evaluate an embedding model on your text data — indispensable to making an informed model choice — without constructing a complex search or RAG pipeline? The most practical pathway to test your model is evaluating how well it separates the original data into meaningful classes or clusters.

Higher scores mean the model does a better job of capturing the nuances that distinguish some vectors (transformed news articles) from others: documents from the same category end up closer together, and further from documents in other categories.

The approximately 0.07 gap between the two models’ scores shows that, when dealing with 500 noisy, messy texts, BGE Small performed much better. A likely reason is that this model has been trained much more strictly and aggressively to turn into a “retrieval specialist”, whereas all-MiniLM-L6-v2 is more generalist and was trained for general-purpose semantic similarity handling: when faced with messy and topic-specific data, it can get overly distracted by shared, boilerplate vocabulary.

This practical guide has been designed to help you understand the nuances and trade-offs of embedding models, based on aspects like dimensionality, token limits, and quantization approaches. It has been accompanied by an example benchmarking between two models, using a noisy dataset of newsgroup posts categorized by topic. Relying on local, open-source tools like sentence-transformers is, at the time of writing, a practical way to find an embedding model that genuinely understands the uniqueness of your text data.
